This page summarises the quantum-chemical theory underlying hftest. For full derivations the reader is referred to the canonical texts [Szabo1989], [HJO2000], and [Cramer2004].

The Electronic Schrödinger Equation

Within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation the nuclei are treated as fixed classical point charges. The goal is to solve

(1)\[\hat{H}_\text{el}\, \Psi = E_\text{el}\, \Psi\]

for the N-electron wave function \(\Psi\), where

\[\hat{H}_\text{el} = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_i^2 - \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{A=1}^M \frac{Z_A}{r_{iA}} + \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j>i}^N \frac{1}{r_{ij}}.\]

The total energy (observable) is

\[E_\text{total} = E_\text{el} + E_\text{nuc}\,,\qquad E_\text{nuc} = \sum_{A < B} \frac{Z_A Z_B}{R_{AB}}\,.\]

The Hartree-Fock Approximation

HF approximates \(\Psi\) by a single Slater determinant:

\[\Psi_\text{HF} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}}\det\!\bigl[\chi_1\chi_2\cdots\chi_N\bigr]\]

where \(\chi_i\) are spin orbitals — products of a spatial orbital \(\phi_i(\mathbf{r})\) and a spin function (\(\alpha\) or \(\beta\)).

The variational principle applied to this determinant yields the Hartree-Fock equations

(2)\[\hat{F}\,\phi_i = \varepsilon_i\,\phi_i\,,\]

where \(\hat{F}\) is the Fock operator

\[\hat{F}(\mathbf{r}_1) = \hat{h}(\mathbf{r}_1) + \sum_{j=1}^N \Bigl[\hat{J}_j(\mathbf{r}_1) - \hat{K}_j(\mathbf{r}_1)\Bigr].\]

The one-electron Hamiltonian \(\hat{h}\) contains kinetic energy and nuclear attraction; \(\hat{J}_j\) is the Coulomb operator (mean-field repulsion) and \(\hat{K}_j\) is the non-local exchange operator (a pure quantum-mechanical effect with no classical analogue).

LCAO Expansion and the Roothaan Equations

Molecular orbitals are expanded in a finite atomic-orbital (AO) basis \(\{\mu\}\) of size \(N_b\):

\[\phi_i(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{\mu=1}^{N_b} C_{\mu i}\,\chi_\mu(\mathbf{r}).\]

Substituting into (2) and projecting onto the basis gives the Roothaan-Hall (closed-shell) or Pople-Nesbet (open-shell) matrix equations:

(3)\[\mathbf{F}\,\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{S}\,\mathbf{C}\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\]

where \(\mathbf{S}_{\mu\nu} = \langle\mu|\nu\rangle\) is the AO overlap matrix, \(\mathbf{C}\) is the MO coefficient matrix, and \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) is diagonal with orbital energies.

The Fock matrix in the AO basis is

\[F_{\mu\nu} = H^{\rm core}_{\mu\nu} + \sum_{\lambda\sigma} P_{\lambda\sigma} \Bigl[(\mu\nu|\lambda\sigma) - \tfrac{1}{2}(\mu\sigma|\lambda\nu)\Bigr]\]

where \((\mu\nu|\lambda\sigma) = \iint \chi_\mu(\mathbf{r}_1)\chi_\nu(\mathbf{r}_1)\,\frac{1}{r_{12}}\, \chi_\lambda(\mathbf{r}_2)\chi_\sigma(\mathbf{r}_2)\, d\mathbf{r}_1\,d\mathbf{r}_2\) are the two-electron repulsion integrals (ERIs), and the density matrix is

\[P_{\mu\nu} = 2\sum_{i=1}^{N/2} C_{\mu i} C_{\nu i} \quad \text{(closed-shell, RHF)}.\]

Electronic Energy

For RHF the converged electronic energy is

\[E_\text{el} = \tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl[ \mathbf{P}\bigl(\mathbf{H}^{\rm core} + \mathbf{F}\bigr)\bigr].\]

Restricted vs Unrestricted HF

Restricted Hartree-Fock (RHF)

All electrons occupy paired spatial orbitals: \(\alpha\)- and \(\beta\)-spin electrons of the same pair share the same spatial function. RHF is only applicable to closed-shell (singlet) systems. It leads to the single Fock matrix above.

Unrestricted Hartree-Fock (UHF)

\(\alpha\)- and \(\beta\)-spin electrons use independent sets of spatial orbitals \(\{\phi_i^\alpha\}\) and \(\{\phi_j^\beta\}\).

The separate density matrices are

\[P^\alpha_{\mu\nu} = \sum_{i=1}^{N_\alpha} C^\alpha_{\mu i} C^\alpha_{\nu i}\,,\qquad P^\beta_{\mu\nu} = \sum_{i=1}^{N_\beta} C^\beta_{\mu i} C^\beta_{\nu i}\,,\]

and the two Fock matrices are

\[\begin{split}F^\alpha_{\mu\nu} &= H^{\rm core}_{\mu\nu} + \sum_{\lambda\sigma} \bigl(P^\alpha_{\lambda\sigma}+P^\beta_{\lambda\sigma}\bigr)(\mu\nu|\lambda\sigma) - P^\alpha_{\lambda\sigma}(\mu\sigma|\lambda\nu) \\[4pt] F^\beta_{\mu\nu} &= H^{\rm core}_{\mu\nu} + \sum_{\lambda\sigma} \bigl(P^\alpha_{\lambda\sigma}+P^\beta_{\lambda\sigma}\bigr)(\mu\nu|\lambda\sigma) - P^\beta_{\lambda\sigma}(\mu\sigma|\lambda\nu).\end{split}\]

The electronic energy is

\[E_\text{el} = \tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl[ (\mathbf{P}^\alpha+\mathbf{P}^\beta)\mathbf{H}^{\rm core} + \mathbf{P}^\alpha\mathbf{F}^\alpha + \mathbf{P}^\beta \mathbf{F}^\beta\bigr].\]

Spin Contamination

UHF wave functions are not eigenfunctions of \(\hat{S}^2\) in general. The expectation value

\[\langle\hat{S}^2\rangle_\text{UHF} = S(S+1) + N_\beta - \sum_{i,j} \bigl|\langle\phi^\alpha_i|\phi^\beta_j\rangle\bigl|^2\]

deviates from the exact value \(S(S+1)\) by the spin-contamination term, evaluated from the overlap of occupied alpha and beta MO blocks.

Gaussian Basis Sets

The AO basis functions are contracted Gaussian-type orbitals (cGTOs):

\[\chi_\mu(\mathbf{r}) \propto \underbrace{x^{n_x} y^{n_y} z^{n_z}}_{\text{angular part}}\, \sum_k d_k\, e^{-\alpha_k |\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{A}|^2}\]

where \((n_x,n_y,n_z)\) specifies the Cartesian angular momentum, \(\mathbf{A}\) is the nuclear centre, the \(\alpha_k\) are primitive exponents, and the \(d_k\) are contraction coefficients pre-normalised during basis loading.

The angular quantum number \(\ell = n_x+n_y+n_z\) labels the shell type: \(\ell=0\) (S), \(1\) (P), \(2\) (D), \(3\) (F), \(4\) (G). A shell of angular momentum \(\ell\) contains

\[N_\text{cart}(\ell) = \tfrac{(\ell+1)(\ell+2)}{2}\]

Cartesian basis functions.

Canonical Orthogonalization

Equation (3) is a generalised eigenvalue problem because \(\mathbf{S}\) is not the identity when basis functions overlap. Canonical orthogonalization transforms to an orthonormal basis:

  1. Diagonalise \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top\).

  2. Define \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{-1/2}\), keeping only columns with \(\lambda_i \ge 10^{-8}\) (discarding linearly dependent combinations).

  3. Transform \(\mathbf{F}' = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{F}\mathbf{X}\).

  4. Solve the ordinary eigenvalue problem \(\mathbf{F}'\mathbf{C}' = \mathbf{C}'\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\).

  5. Back-transform \(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{C}'\).
